name: Tobacco
kicker: Cash crop that saved Jamestown · Grown with enslaved labor in the Chesapeake
briefing: Jamestown nearly failed until John Rolfe planted a sweeter kind of tobacco around 1612 and shipped it to England, where it sold for high prices. Soon Virginians were growing it everywhere, even in the streets, and the crop spread across the Chesapeake on the labor of indentured servants and, later, enslaved Africans. Centuries later, in 1964, a report by the U.S. Surgeon General concluded that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This plant’s genus and its best-known chemical are both named for Jean Nicot, a French ambassador who sent it from Portugal to the French royal court around 1560. Native peoples of the Americas had grown it for ceremonies and trade long before Europeans arrived.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe made the cash crop of colonial Virginia.

tossups.p: King James I wrote a 1604 pamphlet called a “Counterblaste” against this substance, describing its use as “loathsome to the eye, hateful to the nose, harmful to the brain, dangerous to the lungs.” Even so, his own colony in Virginia soon grew rich by selling it.
tossups.r: John Rolfe began growing it there around 1612. For 10 points, name this crop, colonial Virginia’s main export.

tossups.p: In 1617, Deputy Governor Samuel Argall found Jamestown’s colonists growing this crop in the town’s streets and marketplace. A few years later, men in the colony used this crop to pay for the voyages of women who came over as brides.
tossups.r: It had first been planted for export by John Rolfe. For 10 points, name this cash crop, which made Virginia rich.

tossups.p: Patrick Henry first became famous arguing the Parson’s Cause, a 1763 case over a law that let Virginia pay its Anglican ministers in cash instead of in this crop after a drought drove up its price. In colonial Virginia, warehouse receipts for this crop were used as money.
tossups.r: Taxes and fines there were often counted in pounds of it. For 10 points, name this cash crop that John Rolfe made Virginia’s first big export.

tossups.p: In January 1964, a report by Surgeon General Luther Terry concluded that smoking cigarettes made from this plant causes lung cancer. The next year, Congress required health warnings on cigarette packages, and in 1971 cigarette ads were banned from television and radio.
tossups.r: Centuries earlier, this crop had been colonial Virginia’s main export. For 10 points, name this plant first grown for export at Jamestown by John Rolfe.

tossups.p: James Buchanan Duke used the Bonsack machine to mass-produce cigarettes and in 1890 formed a giant company that controlled most of the American market for this crop’s products. The Supreme Court broke up that trust in 1911, the same month it broke up Standard Oil.
tossups.r: Duke University is named for his family. For 10 points, name this crop that made Durham, North Carolina, an industrial city.

tossups.p: Colonial planters packed this crop into huge barrels called hogsheads, which were sometimes rolled along “rolling roads” to the docks. A 1730 Virginia law required this crop to be checked at public warehouses before it could be shipped.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cash crop of the Chesapeake colonies, first grown for export by John Rolfe.

tossups.p: Under England’s Navigation Acts, this crop was one of the “enumerated” goods that colonists could ship only to England or other English colonies. In the 1700s, merchants in Glasgow, Scotland, grew rich buying it from Chesapeake planters.
tossups.r: It was first grown for export at Jamestown by John Rolfe. For 10 points, name this crop that made Virginia and Maryland wealthy.

tossups.p: In the 1760s, George Washington stopped growing this crop at Mount Vernon and switched to wheat, partly because it wore out the soil and left him in debt to British merchants. Many Virginia planters moved west as this crop exhausted their land.
tossups.r: It was the main cash crop of colonial Virginia. For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe first grew for export at Jamestown.

tossups.p: Architect Benjamin Latrobe designed column tops inside the U.S. Capitol decorated with ears of corn, and others decorated with the leaves and flowers of this plant. Before the Revolution, this crop had been the most valuable export of the thirteen colonies.
tossups.r: It grew mostly in Virginia and Maryland. For 10 points, name this cash crop that John Rolfe made famous in Virginia.

tossups.p: Virginia’s headright system gave fifty acres of land for each person whose passage a planter paid, so planters brought over indentured servants to grow this crop. After Bacon’s Rebellion in 1676, planters relied more and more on enslaved Africans instead.
tossups.r: John Rolfe had begun growing it around 1612. For 10 points, name this crop that dominated the economy of the Chesapeake colonies.

tossups.p: The Powhatan people grew a harsh-tasting kind of this plant that English buyers disliked, so Virginia had little to sell until a sweeter species grown from seeds from Spanish colonies was planted around 1612. That sweeter kind soon sold for high prices in London.
tossups.r: Its grower later married Pocahontas. For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe planted to save Jamestown.

tossups.p: In the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement, 46 states settled lawsuits against the largest companies selling cigarettes made from this plant, which agreed to pay more than 200 billion dollars over 25 years and to limit their advertising.
tossups.r: Decades earlier, a 1964 Surgeon General’s report had linked smoking to lung cancer. For 10 points, name this crop, the main cash crop of colonial Virginia.

tossups.p: In 1839, an enslaved blacksmith named Stephen is credited with discovering a way to cure this crop over charcoal fires that turned its leaves bright yellow. That “bright leaf” variety helped make Durham, North Carolina, a center of the industry built on this crop.
tossups.r: Kentucky became a leading grower of its burley variety. For 10 points, name this crop that John Rolfe first grew for export in Virginia.

tossups.p: In November 1492, two members of Christopher Columbus’s crew exploring Cuba saw Taíno [“tah-EE-noh”] people rolling dried leaves of this plant and smoking them. By 1600, Spanish colonies in the Caribbean and South America were growing it for sale in Europe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plant that John Rolfe made the cash crop of colonial Virginia.

trap.title: Which cash crop?
trap.body: Colonial-economy questions often ask for a crop, and four answers get mixed up. Tobacco was the cash crop of Virginia and Maryland, starting with John Rolfe at Jamestown. Rice and indigo were the big crops of colonial South Carolina, where Eliza Lucas Pinckney grew indigo in the 1740s. Cotton took over the Deep South only after Eli Whitney’s cotton gin (1793), and sugar was king in the Caribbean.
trap.fix: Rolfe, Jamestown, the Chesapeake, hogsheads, King James’s “Counterblaste,” the Parson’s Cause, the Dukes of Durham, and the 1964 Surgeon General’s report mean tobacco. Eliza Lucas means indigo, the cotton gin and “King Cotton” mean cotton, and Caribbean plantations usually mean sugar.
